commentary_segments.text: As bandgap reference voltages are always 1.2 V, we can wonder how to achieve a reference voltage with value below 1 V. Indeed, the only physical constant available is this bandgap voltage. How can the properties of this bandgap voltage be exploited at lower supply voltages? The answer will lie in the conversion of this bandgap reference voltage into currents, which are then summed up to lower output reference voltages. The requirement on the supply voltage will be that we need at least one single V and some mV’s. We can bias the bipolar transistor at very low currents, which may yield BE V values down to 0.5 V. In this case, a minimum supply voltage could be reached of the same BE order of magnitude.

Indeed, the only physical constant available is this bandgap voltage. How can the properties of this bandgap voltage be exploited at lower supply voltages? The answer will lie in the conversion of this bandgap reference voltage into currents, which are then summed up to lower output reference voltages. The requirement on the supply voltage will be that we need at least one single V and some mV’s. We can bias the bipolar transistor at very low currents, which may yield BE V values down to 0.5 V. In this case, a minimum supply voltage could be reached of the same BE order of magnitude.
